analysis.one_liner: Overhauls credit report disputes, gives free credit scores, limits medical debt reporting, and bans most employer credit checks.
analysis.headline: The bill — sponsored by one member with a single cosponsor — sat in the House Financial Services Committee for 18 months without a hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for the companies that compile credit reports. It would force credit bureaus to genuinely investigate disputes and give consumers a right to appeal, provide free credit scores alongside free annual reports, limit medical debt on credit reports, and ban most employers from checking applicants' credit. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers would gain the most: the bill would force credit bureaus to genuinely investigate disputes, give consumers a right to appeal, and stop bureaus from dismissing disputes as frivolous [S3]. Consumers would get free credit scores with their free annual reports, and lenders would have to show applicants the report and score used to deny or price a loan before they sign [S2]. People with medical debt — nearly one in five consumers — would see medical collections kept off or removed from their reports [S3]. Job applicants would no longer have most employers checking their credit [S3]. Extra protections would go to servicemembers, identity theft and fraud victims, and survivors of financial abuse by a partner [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with credit errors and medical debt

how_it_helps.text: Requires credit bureaus to conduct independent investigations of disputes, pass consumers' evidence along to data furnishers, and stop dismissing disputes as frivolous, with a new right to appeal the result
Gives consumers free credit scores with their free annual credit reports and requires lenders to show applicants the report and score used in an underwriting decision before they sign the loan

Limits the medical debt that can appear on credit reports and speeds removal of fully paid or settled debt, addressing research cited in the bill that medical collections unfairly depress scores by 10 to 22 points and affect nearly one-fifth of consumers
Bans the use of credit information in most employment decisions, ending what the bill's findings call a catch-22 in which job loss damages credit and damaged credit then blocks getting a new job

Adds protections for servicemembers, identity theft and fraud victims, and survivors of financial abuse, including free credit monitoring for certain consumers and easier removal of fraudulent information

Bans automatic renewals and misleading marketing of credit report and score products, codifying practices the Consumer Bureau had already forced the three big bureaus to stop through consent orders and fines totaling tens of millions of dollars

analysis.who_pays: The three nationwide credit bureaus (Equifax, TransUnion, and Experian) would bear new compliance costs — detailed dispute-investigation standards, a nationwide registry, cybersecurity examinations, and bans on auto-renewing subscription sales — and would lose revenue from selling credit scores and monitoring subscriptions [S3]. Debt collectors and debt buyers would lose the ability to report much medical debt and would have to remove paid or settled debts quickly [S3]. Lenders and other furnishers would face new record-keeping and notice duties [S3]. Employers would lose the ability to check most job applicants' credit history [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and lenders

drawbacks.text: Furnishers of credit data — lenders, collectors, even utilities and landlords reporting payments — would face new record-keeping, notice, and investigation duties, and those compliance costs could be passed to borrowers or make some lenders report less information at all

Quickly deleting paid, settled, and medical debts removes information lenders use to price risk, which could lead lenders to tighten credit or raise prices for other borrowers to cover the added uncertainty
Employers lose credit screening that, as the bill's own findings note, some organizations use to reduce theft and embezzlement risk; the bill bans it for most roles even for positions handling money

The bill is broad — roughly ten titles touching disputes, scores, student loans, employment, marketing, and cybersecurity — and its cost estimates and implementation burden were never publicly examined because no hearing was ever held

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — fixing a dispute process the bill's own findings describe as rigged toward speed over accuracy, with staff at one big bureau given five minutes per dispute — addresses a real, documented harm that falls on ordinary people, and the free-score and medical-debt provisions attack practices regulators had already penalized. The costs are real but ordinary: compliance burdens on lenders and bureaus, some loss of underwriting information, and the loss of credit checks for employers. The bill was never costed or refined in committee, so its weakest edges — like banning employer credit checks with narrow exceptions — went unexamined. On balance it would have shifted power and cost from consumers to the credit data industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day
The referral was the bill's only action of record; the committee never held a markup or hearing on it, and it never reached the House floor
The bill attracted just one cosponsor, a House Democrat, over the entire Congress

The bill's findings cited a federal study finding that 26 percent of consumers had at least one potentially material error on their credit report, and Consumer Bureau data showing medical collections appear on the reports of nearly one-fifth of all consumers
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all pending legislation died with it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The three nationwide credit bureaus and other companies that furnish or sell credit data are better off: they never had to comply with the stricter dispute rules, free-score mandates, or marketing restrictions, and employers kept the ability to check applicants' credit. Consumers with credit report errors, medical debt, or bad-credit job rejections gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, debt collectors, and employers

for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill — no markup, hearing, or floor scheduling — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded support was from House Democrats — the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would impose detailed dispute-handling standards, require free credit scores, ban auto-renewing subscription sales, and create a registry and cybersecurity exams for large bureaus — cutting into the paid score and monitoring products that are a growing part of their business.
The bill would sharply limit medical debt collections on reports and require expedited removal of fully paid or settled debts, shrinking the leverage collectors get from what they can report.

industries.industry: Private student loan holders and servicers
industries.note: The bill would require them to hand borrowers their report and score before signing and to remove adverse information for certain distressed borrowers, weakening the bad-credit penalty they rely on.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and identity-theft protection providers
industries.note: The bill would give certain consumers free credit monitoring and identity theft protection, competing directly with paid subscription products that cost consumers roughly $120 to $300 a year.

industries.industry: Employers that use credit checks in hiring
industries.note: The bill would prohibit the use of credit information in most hiring decisions, taking away a screening tool used by 60 percent of employers by 2011, according to findings cited in the bill.
